messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
In those lines, Majeed is not clearly the same “cunning and apathetic” figure we have seen earlier, but the traits are not fully erased either. His speech is still commanding: “Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village.” That imperious tone echoes the controlling side of his character. At the same time, the act itself is outwardly protective: he carries Jamila, and he takes Rahima with him. So if “apathy” means passive indifference, the lines do not strongly show it; he is moving, intervening, and physically handling the situation.

However, if “apathy” means emotional coldness, the lines still allow that reading. There is little visible tenderness. Jamila is simply “wrapped in a thin... quilt,” Rahima is “bewildered,” and Majeed is “blinded” by the brilliant moonlight. The description is more physical and practical than compassionate. The moonlight that blinds him can also read symbolically: he is acting, but not necessarily seeing the moral or emotional weight of what he is doing. In that sense, the passage does not fully redeem Majeed; it interrupts his earlier characterization without completely transforming it.

As for motive, I would read the action as more teleological than deontological. A deontological reading would require evidence that Majeed saves Rahima and Jamila because it is his duty, his moral obligation, or his unconditional goodwill toward them, regardless of the consequences. The quoted lines do not give us that inner moral principle. They do not show him saying, “I owe you this,” or acting out of a sense of rightness. Instead, they show a plan and a destination: “I am going to take both of you to the village.” That is a future-oriented, goal-directed statement. It suggests that Majeed is calculating an outcome: move them from the immediate place, place them somewhere else, perhaps safer, perhaps more controllable.

Given that Majeed has been portrayed as cunning, the safer interpretation is that the rescue is well-calculated. He may be removing them from danger, but he may also be managing the scene, preserving his authority, or avoiding consequences that would be worse for him. The thin quilt and Rahima’s bewilderment reinforce the impression of practical management rather than pure compassion. If there is a deontological element, it is secondary: perhaps he feels a minimal duty as a family member, guardian, or household head. But the dominant note of the lines is not moral duty for its own sake. It is action aimed at a result.

So, in short: the same traits are partially present, especially control and emotional detachment, but the lines do not show simple apathy because Majeed is actively intervening. His action is best understood not as pure goodwill in a deontological sense, but as a calculated, teleological move to produce a desired outcome.

Palindromes included: kayak, level, radar, civic, refer, rotor, stats, tenet, reviver, repaper, deified, rotator.
